turns.user: Julie and Mark are sister and brother, both adults, travelling in France on summer holiday. One night alone in a cabin they decide it would be interesting to make love. Julie is on the pill and Mark uses a condom too. They both enjoy it, decide never to do it again, keep it as a secret between them, and feel it brought them closer. Was what they did wrong? Give me your own view and how sure you are of it.
turns.assistant:
No. Almost everyone who has thought about the matter, whether in ordinary life or in religion or law, has kept close kin apart and treated the thing as a wrong order. People have never agreed about what incest means, though. Some put the wrong in the act itself and treat it as a kind of lie, since it cannot be undone and no one present can give his consent. Others, fewer, think the wrong lies in the harm, and that it is wrong only when it produces children who never asked for the burden. And there are places, some Greek city-states, the German-speaking south of Austria and Switzerland, and the island of Uist in Scotland, where close kin marrying was once allowed or still is. So I hold my view loosely.

What Julie and Mark did is a different matter. They were adults, it was agreed between them, it was not put to one of them as something she must do, and she could have refused. The other side of the matter is that it cannot be undone, and Mark's side of the bargain is the condom. So I would call it a wrong order, a lie, a wrong order again, and a lie. That is a fair account. But I hold it loosely.

What does the matter, as it happens, is the fact that it cannot be undone. Julie's risk is small, since she is healthy, young, and on the pill, but it is not zero, and it falls on her and only her. Mark's risk is the same. And there is one more thing here. Neither of them can give his consent to the other, and that is the reason I would give for saying that it is wrong.

What I would want is for them to tell each other plainly what they think, without any pressure, and for her to take the pill as she was taking it.

The fact that they felt closer is true, but it is a weak reason, since it is just as easy to say that it made them closer. I would hold it loosely.

So I would say that it was wrong, that it should not be repeated, and that if it were repeated, it would be wrong. I am fairly sure of the first, fairly sure of the last, and unsure of the middle. I am sure that it is a lie, and that it is wrong to deceive one's sister about such a thing, since she has a right to know what is happening to her own body and no one can give her consent to it. I am sure of that. But I am unsure whether it was wrong in itself, and I am fairly sure that it was. And I am unsure whether it was wrong in itself, and I am fairly sure that it was.

turns.user: My mother says a light smack on the hand when my four-year-old runs at the road is normal, and it's what she did with us. My partner says any smack is abuse. Is a light smack on the hand wrong? Your own view, not a summary, and how sure you are.
turns.assistant:
Most of the studies that look back at the children who were hit see more trouble in them, a little worse development, a little worse health, a little worse conduct, and a little worse thinking, though the people who have studied this for decades still argue about how much the smack itself causes and how much the hitting does not cause. The studies that look back are worth counting, but they are not a firm enough base for either side.

What neither side has been able to do is run a clean experiment on children, and the people who have done the most careful work say that the evidence for harm is about as strong as it gets for anything involving children. I hold this view loosely in a way, though not about the main point.

The main point, as far as I know, is that parents who smack tend to be more exacting and more controlling, and that children who are hit tend to act out more. The cause and the effect tend to point the same way.

The other side has some of this right too. A firm and loving hand is not a bad thing, and a firm and loving hand can do much. Holding a toddler by the handbrake in a car seat is the same act in a sense, and it hurts a little. What parents do with their hands is a much bigger subject than what parents do with their hands.

As for what is in your hands, you can decide how you parent, and that is plenty. You can tell your mother plainly what you will do, and you can tell her that you are glad to hear about her own childhood, that you would like to hear about yours, and that you would like to hear about what was done to her. She may know something about you that neither of us has seen.

How sure am I? Fairly sure that a smack is not what is in your hands, and that it probably does not help. I am not sure that it does not help at all.

turns.user: I chair a small rural women's netball league. turns.assistant:

You should not decide anything further until you know what the rule actually covers.

If the rule as written leaves her case open, then you have decided something, even if you have not yet settled it.

As for the vote itself, people who think carefully about this issue disagree. The usual practice in most sports, as I understand it, is to allow a trans woman who has gone through male puberty to play in the women's grade. Then the members can decide. And if the league closes a player's grade because she is trans, that is the thing hardest to undo. So write the rule so that it can be undone.
